chapter_theme: The one song at Poovalur (பூவாளூர்) in the rain-fed land of the Kaveri's channels: a catalogue of murderous, money-asking courtesans, and praise that makes Murugan the child-saint who defeated the Jains of Madurai and saved the Pandya king and queen.

920.reading: The poet lists courtesans whose eyes are Death's arrows, saw-blades and poison, murderous sinners who recite the Kama-shastra, question any lover, are vessels of pleasure, ask for coins, are shapes of illusion, and charge with breasts like elephants, and asks whether he should waste time with them; he asks for the day Murugan will say 'come' and rule him with love. The praise is Sambandar's story: the mouth still wet with the Goddess's milk sang, the palm leaf went against the current, eight thousand Jains lost the debate and mounted the stakes, the Tamil land that had abandoned the ash was saved, and the king whose hunch was straightened and his queen were made to live at Alavai; Murugan is that child of jnana, at Poovalur.
920.nuance: காசு கேட்டிடும் மாயா ரூபிகள, those who ask for coins, mark the courtesans. In the praise every detail is Sambandar's: பால் அறாத் திருவாய் (the infant fed by the Goddess), ஏடு நீர்க்கு எதிர் போய் (the leaf in the Vaigai), இரு நாலாம் ஆயிர சமண் (eight thousand Jains), கூன் நிமிர் இறையோன் (the Pandya cured of his hunch). The queen is not named; tradition calls her Mangaiyarkkarasi. நீறிடாத் தமிழ்நாடு, the Tamil land without the ash, is the poet's word for the Jain period.

links.note: Both make Murugan the saint who cured the Pandya's hunch and sent the Jains to the stake; 306 sets it against court poetry, 920 against the courtesans, and adds the leaf against the current and the queen who lived on at Alavai.
